value.summary: Socrates argues that since justice is the soul's excellence, the just person lives well and is happy, rendering justice more profitable than injustice. However, he concludes with self-dissatisfaction, noting that jumping between questions left the fundamental nature of justice unknown.

nodes.label: Justice as Excellence of Soul
nodes.summary: Justice is acknowledged as the excellence of the soul, while injustice is its defect.
nodes.speaker: Socrates
nodes.rationale: Direct premise stated as an agreed claim about the nature of justice and the soul.

nodes.label: Just Soul Lives Well and Happy
nodes.summary: Because the just soul lives well, the just person is blessed and happy, whereas the unjust person is miserable.
nodes.speaker: Socrates
nodes.rationale: Deductive claim built upon the excellence of the soul.

nodes.label: Superior Profit of Justice
nodes.summary: Since happiness is profitable and misery is not, injustice can never be more profitable than justice.
nodes.speaker: Socrates
nodes.rationale: Conclusive argument synthesizing happiness and profitability against Thrasymachus's position.

nodes.label: Editorial Note on Socrates
nodes.summary: An editorial sidenote records that Socrates is displeased with himself and with the argument.
nodes.rationale: Paratextual/editorial comment summarizing Socrates' state of mind.

nodes.label: Socrates' Aporia and Self-Blame
nodes.summary: Socrates blames himself for wandering into downstream questions before defining the nature of justice, concluding that he knows nothing.
nodes.speaker: Socrates
nodes.rationale: Reflective argument evaluating the methodology of the entire dialogue's inquiry.

edges.rationale: Justice being the soul's excellence grounds the inference that the just soul lives well and is happy.
The premise that the just person is happy and happiness is profitable leads to the conclusion that justice is more profitable than injustice.
Socrates' self-critique questions the validity of concluding about the comparative profit or happiness of justice before defining its nature.
